lines.text: """Return applied IDs a staging rollback must keep: retained closure (G2).
`retain` is already known to be applied (journal read it), so this is a
pure graph closure: starting from the retained IDs, walk prerequisite and
keep every node reached that is in `applied`. Walking only through
*applied* prerequisites matters -- an unapplied prerequisite was never
released, so it cannot be un-released and must not widen the kept set
(and emitting it would break G1's rollback-only-applied rule).
Keeping ancestors is required for correctness, not politeness: a retained
consumer still needs its library, so rolling the library back underneath
it would leave the surviving release broken.
The order comes from `changes`/`applied` only, never from the retain list's
own order, so the emitted sequence stays the single deterministic reverse
topological order and is reproducible across calls.

lines.text: def read_retain(value):
"""Validate a staging rollback's retain list; return it in request order.
retain is a rollback-only field (CHANGE-G2.md:7): planner.py calls this only
on the rollback path, so a malformed retain on a plan request must never
raise invalid-retain nor change the plan result. The shape rules mirror the
journal (non-array, null, empty string or non-string element) but use their
own code, and a missing field defaults to empty. Membership in `applied` is
not checked here because retain's legal values depend on replay state that
planner.py holds; if it is not an applied ID, planner.py rejects it.
Callers pass request.get("retain", []) so an absent field means nothing is
retained (all applied changes roll back, exactly as in G1). Rejections are
JournalError("invalid-retain") so the request still yields the shared error
envelope instead of partial actions.
